audits.title: 1845. Implementing Outpatient Antimicrobial Stewardship in a Primary Care Office Through Pharmacist-led Audit and Feedback
audits.standard: ASP guidelines for URI and UTI treatment
audits.setting: Outpatient primary care office, Mercy Health Saint Mary's, Grand Rapids

cycle1.result: Fluoroquinolone prescribing for UTI 85%; median URI duration 10 days.

audits.intervention: Education with pocket cards on URI and UTI guidelines, then weekly pharmacist audit of all antibiotics for URI/UTI with feedback to prescribers.

cycle2.result: Fluoroquinolone prescribing for UTI fell to 40% in month 1 and 11.7% over the next 6 months; median URI duration 7 days.

audits.other_findings: Nitrofurantoin rose from 0.4% to 38.6% of UTI prescriptions; commonest feedback reasons were inappropriate agent (26.3%) and too long a duration (24.3%).
audits.citation: Burns K, Pham S, Dumkow L, Egwuatu N. 1845. Implementing Outpatient Antimicrobial Stewardship in a Primary Care Office Through Pharmacist-led Audit and Feedback. Open Forum Infect Dis. 2018;5(Suppl 1):S527-S527.

audits.title: [Antibiotic treatment of infections in general practice. Effect of audit assessed by prescriptions data from health insurance registry and physicians' own registration].
audits.standard: Locally prepared treatment guidelines for infections
audits.setting: General practices in the County of Roskilde

cycle1.result: 47.2% of patients did not receive antibiotics.

audits.intervention: Audit with course participation and preparation of treatment guidelines.

cycle2.result: 52.4% of patients did not receive antibiotics (significant increase).

audits.other_findings: Registry data showed a shift to narrow-spectrum penicillin but this was also seen in non-participating GPs; 46 GPs took part.
audits.citation: Damsgaard JJ, Schaefer K, Michelsen JW, Frimodt-Møller N, Munck AP, Vach K, et al.. [Antibiotic treatment of infections in general practice. Effect of audit assessed by prescriptions data from health insurance registry and physicians' own registration]. Ugeskr Laeger. 2001;163(2):165-168. PMID: 11379242.

audits.title: A retrospective audit of antibiotic prescriptions in primary health-care facilities in Eastern Region, Ghana.
audits.standard: WHO/International Network for the Rational Use of Drugs rational drug use indicators
audits.setting: Four public and private primary health-care facilities, Eastern Region, Ghana

cycle1.result: Mean 4.01 medicines per encounter; 59.9% of prescriptions had antibiotics and 24.2% injections; 79.2% of medicines were generics and 88.1% from the national essential medicines list.

audits.other_findings: 400 prescriptions sampled per facility; facility type, age, number of medicines, no malaria drug and upper respiratory tract infection diagnosis were associated with antibiotic prescription.
audits.citation: Ahiabu MA, Tersbøl BP, Biritwum R, Bygbjerg IC, Magnussen P. A retrospective audit of antibiotic prescriptions in primary health-care facilities in Eastern Region, Ghana. Health Policy Plan. 2016;31(2):250-258. doi:10.1093/heapol/czv048. PMID: 26045328.

audits.title: Antibiotic Prescription Audits Among Pediatric Outpatients With Acute Ailments in a Secondary Care Hospital During the COVID-19 Omicron Wave in Northern India.
audits.setting: Outpatient department of a private paediatric hospital, Kanpur

cycle1.result: Antibiotic prescription rate 65.75%, higher than WHO-recommended value; none of 144 antibiotics prescribed generically; all prescribed presumptively.

audits.other_findings: Commonest antibiotics were cefpodoxime, azithromycin and ofloxacin, mainly for cough and stomach infections.
audits.citation: Sodhi B, Basu S. Antibiotic Prescription Audits Among Pediatric Outpatients With Acute Ailments in a Secondary Care Hospital During the COVID-19 Omicron Wave in Northern India. Cureus. 2022;14(11):e32017. doi:10.7759/cureus.32017. PMID: 36589166.

audits.title: An audit of antibiotic prescribing in primary care 2019-2020 in Dunmanway Primary Care Centre.
audits.standard: HSE Guidelines for Antimicrobial Prescribing in Primary Care; 90% compliance for choice, 70% for dose and course
audits.intervention: Educational intervention with texts, information and review of current guidelines
audits.other_findings: Course compliance fell below standard at re-audit; delayed scripts 10% vs 4.2%; co-amoxiclav 17.5% vs 12.5%.

audits.title: Implementing outpatient antimicrobial stewardship in a primary care office through ambulatory care pharmacist-led audit and feedback.
audits.standard: Guideline-concordant antibiotic agent and duration for upper respiratory and urinary tract infections
audits.setting: Primary care office within a health system

cycle1.result: Guideline-concordant agent for UTI 20% and duration 55%; guideline-concordant agent for URI 43.3%; median URI duration 10 days.

audits.intervention: Education and guidelines followed by bi-weekly pharmacist audit of all URI and UTI prescriptions with written feedback to prescribers.

cycle2.result: Guideline-concordant agent for UTI median 69.2% and duration 70.4%; URI agent 86.8%; median URI duration 7 days.

audits.other_findings: Commonest feedback reasons were inappropriate agent (26.3%) and prolonged duration (24.3%).
audits.citation: Burns KW, Johnson KM, Pham SN, Egwuatu NE, Dumkow LE. Implementing outpatient antimicrobial stewardship in a primary care office through ambulatory care pharmacist-led audit and feedback. J Am Pharm Assoc (2003). 2020;60(6):e246-e251. doi:10.1016/j.japh.2020.08.003. PMID: 32861616.

audits.title: Improving primary care antimicrobial stewardship by implementing a peer audit and feedback intervention in Cape Town community healthcare centres.
audits.standard: Bundle of seven antibiotic process measures based on Standard Treatment Guidelines and Essential Medicines List
audits.setting: 10 primary care centres, Cape Town metropole

cycle1.period: First 6 months of July 2017 to June 2019 study

audits.intervention: Monthly multidisciplinary peer audit and feedback of 10 random antibiotic prescriptions, Excel scoring tools, consumption feedback and twice-yearly learning collaboratives
audits.other_findings: Antibiotic consumption was monitored as defined daily doses per 100 prescriptions.

audits.title: Self-audit of prescribing habits and clinical care in general practice.

cycle1.result: Inappropriate prescribing identified for fungal skin infections and coughs and colds in children.

audits.intervention: Self-audit of prescribing using encounter forms.

cycle2.result: More appropriate prescribing reduced number of drugs prescribed and repeat consultations.

audits.other_findings: Encounter forms were used continuously over three years.

audits.title: An audit of high oral broad-spectrum antibiotic prescribing within a Bristol-based general practice
audits.standard: 0% of oral broad-spectrum antibiotics prescribed inappropriately (outside regional guidance without specialist input or evidence of infection)
audits.setting: Downend Health Group, Bristol; general practice; patients over 60

cycle1.result: 107 (51%) prescriptions inappropriate: 63 (30%) wrong antibiotic choice, 44 (21%) no evidence of infection.

audits.intervention: Planned: clinical governance meeting, updated EMIS alerts and antimicrobial stewardship protocols, re-audit 7 months later.
audits.other_findings: Top inappropriate indications were UTI (22%), diverticulitis without pyrexia (15%) and cellulitis (11%); remote consultations had more inappropriate prescribing; 15 of 20 (75%) non-GP prescriptions inappropriate.
audits.citation: Chan C, Shah P. An audit of high oral broad-spectrum antibiotic prescribing within a Bristol-based general practice. International Journal of Pharmacy Practice. 2022;30(Supplement_2):ii12-ii13. doi:10.1093/ijpp/riac089.013.
